subject: Biology
title: Hibernation and Torpor
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Hibernation and Torpor.

hook.text: A hibernating ground squirrel's body drops to near freezing. Its heart beats once every few minutes.

buildup.text: Hibernation is a deep, prolonged state of reduced metabolism to survive winter food scarcity.

discovery.text: Bears aren't true hibernators—they enter a lighter torpor and can wake quickly if disturbed.

twist.text: Hummingbirds enter torpor every night, dropping body temperature by 30°C to save energy.

climax.text: Scientists study hibernation for clues to keeping human organs viable for longer transplant times.

punchline.text: Sleep through winter. Wake up when food returns.

quiz.question: Are bears true hibernators?
options: No—they enter a lighter state called torpor
No—they stay fully awake all winter

details.summary: Hibernation is a state of dramatically reduced metabolism that allows animals to survive long periods without food during winter. Heart rate, breathing, and body temperature plummet. Torpor is a shorter version, lasting hours to days rather than months.
details.whyItMatters: Hibernation demonstrates extreme physiological flexibility. Research into how hibernators survive near-freezing body temperatures without organ damage has implications for human medicine, including hypothermic surgery and organ preservation.
takeaways: Hibernating ground squirrels drop body temperature near freezing
Torpor provides daily energy savings for hummingbirds and small mammals
Hibernators periodically rewarm to enter normal sleep during winter

faq.question: Is hibernation just long sleep?
faq.answer: No. Hibernation involves fundamentally different physiology from sleep. Body temperature drops dramatically, metabolism falls to as low as 2 percent of normal, and brain activity is minimal. Hibernators actually need to wake up periodically to sleep normally.

faq.question: Do bears truly hibernate?
faq.answer: Bears enter a lighter form called winter lethargy. Their temperature drops only a few degrees, and they can wake quickly if disturbed. True deep hibernators like ground squirrels experience much more extreme metabolic suppression.
